Cover:
1. Numbers: are they echoed verbatim from the input token, or reformatted? Test integers, floats, exponent forms (1e10, 1E10, 1e+10, 3.0e2), negative, -0, leading zeros are invalid JSON so check the error, very long digit strings, very large/small exponents, 1.0, 0.30000000000000004, huge ints beyond int64/float64. Determine precisely whether any normalization happens.
2. Booleans and null.
3. Strings: determine the EXACT escaping rules for output. Do a systematic sweep of every code point that matters. Suggested method: use python3 to generate JSON containing one code point per key, run gron, and diff against your model. Check: which chars get short escapes (\\b \\f \\n \\r \\t \\" \\\\), which get \\uXXXX (and whether hex digits are UPPER or lower case), which pass through literally. Test all of 0x00-0xFF plus U+0100, U+00A0, U+2028, U+2029, U+2027, U+202A, U+FEFF, U+FFFD, U+FFFF, U+10000, U+10FFFF, and unpaired surrogates written as \\uD800 in the input.
   Also test whether '<' '>' '&' are escaped, whether '/' is escaped, and whether input escapes like \\u0041 are decoded and re-encoded (i.e. is the output canonicalized?).
4. Invalid UTF-8 bytes in the input string (raw bytes, not escapes) - what comes out? Test a lone 0x80, 0xC3 with no continuation, overlong encodings, truncated multi-byte at EOF.
5. Empty string, string that is only escapes.
6. What does the LHS look like for a nested empty object/array vs a non-empty one - confirm the exact placeholder text used ({} and []) and confirm containers always get their own statement.

content.content:
# gron

Make JSON greppable!

gron transforms JSON into discrete assignments to make it easier to `grep` for what you want and see the absolute 'path' to it.
It eases the exploration of APIs that return large blobs of JSON but have terrible documentation.

## Example

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author"
json[0].commit.author = {};
json[0].commit.author.date = "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z";
json[0].commit.author.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
json[0].commit.author.name = "Tom Hudson";
```

gron can work backwards too, enabling you to turn your filtered data back into JSON:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "commit": {
      "author": {
        "date": "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z",
        "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
        "name": "Tom Hudson"
      }
    }
  }
]
```

## Usage

Get JSON from a file:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json 
json = {};
json.contact = {};
json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
json.github = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/";
json.likes = [];
json.likes[0] = "code";
json.likes[1] = "cheese";
json.likes[2] = "meat";
json.name = "Tom";
```

From a URL:

```
▶ gron http://headers.jsontest.com/
json = {};
json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
json["User-Agent"] = "gron/0.1";
json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "6917a823919477919dbc1523584ba25d/11970839830843610056";
```

Or from `stdin`:

```
▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron
json = {};
json.Accept = "*/*";
json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
json["User-Agent"] = "curl/7.43.0";
json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147";
```

Grep for something and easily see the path to it:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep twitter
json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
```

gron makes diffing JSON easy too:

```
▶ diff <(gron two.json) <(gron two-b.json)
3c3
< json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
---
> json.contact.email = "contact@tomnomnom.com";
```

The output of `gron` is valid JavaScript:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json > tmp.js
▶ echo "console.log(json);" >> tmp.js
▶ nodejs tmp.js
{ contact: { email: 'mail@tomnomnom.com', twitter: '@TomNomNom' },
  github: 'https://github.com/tomnomnom/',
  likes: [ 'code', 'cheese', 'meat' ],
  name: 'Tom' }
```

It's also possible to obtain the `gron` output as JSON stream via the `--json` switch:

```
▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron --json
[[],{}]
[["Accept"],"*/*"]
[["Host"],"headers.jsontest.com"]
[["User-Agent"],"curl/7.43.0"]
[["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"],"c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147"]
```

## ungronning

gron can also turn its output back into JSON:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | gron -u
{
  "contact": {
    "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
    "twitter": "@TomNomNom"
  },
  "github": "https://github.com/tomnomnom/",
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ],
  "name": "Tom"
}
```

This means you can use gron with `grep` and other tools to modify JSON:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

Or with JSON stream mode:

```
▶ gron --json testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --json --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

To preserve array keys, arrays are padded with `null` when values are missing:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese
json.likes = [];
json.likes[0] = "code";
json.likes[2] = "meat";

▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese | gron --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    null,
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

## Command-line Options

```
Transform JSON (from a file, URL, or stdin) into discrete assignments to make it greppable

Usage:
  gron [OPTIONS] [FILE|URL|-]

Options:
  -u, --ungron     Reverse the operation (turn assignments back into JSON)
  -v, --values     Print just the values of provided assignments
  -c, --colorize   Colorize output (default on tty)
  -m, --monochrome Monochrome (don't colorize output)
  -s, --stream     Treat each line of input as a separate JSON object
  -k, --insecure   Disable certificate validation
  -j, --json       Represent gron data as JSON stream
      --no-sort    Don't sort output (faster)
      --version    Print version information

Exit Codes:
  0	OK
  1	Failed to open file
  2	Failed to read input
  3	Failed to form statements
  4	Failed to fetch URL
  5	Failed to parse statements
  6	Failed to encode JSON

Examples:
  gron /tmp/apiresponse.json
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 
  curl -s http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | gron
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | grep company | gron --ungron
```

## Aliases

It's recommended that you alias `ungron` or `norg` (or both!) to `gron --ungron`:

```bash
alias norg="gron --ungron"
alias ungron="gron --ungron"
```

# gron — RHS value rendering in default (gron) mode

Binary under test: `/workspace/executable` (`gron version dev`).
Environment: `NO_COLOR=1`, `TERM=dumb` (so all outputs below are monochrome unless stated).
Scratch dir used: `/tmp/probe/work-01`.

Everything below is about the **VALUE** (right-hand side) of a statement. LHS/path
formatting is out of scope except for §6 (container placeholders).

---

## 0. Statement shape (bytes around the value)

Every statement is exactly:

```
<LHS> SP '=' SP <VALUE> ';' LF
```

i.e. one space before `=`, one space after `=`, then the value, then a single `;`
and a single `\n` (0x0A). There is **always** a trailing newline after the last
statement; there is no trailing blank line. Verified with `od -c`:

```
$ printf '{"b":" "}' > hx.json && /workspace/executable hx.json | od -c
0000000   j   s   o   n       =       {   }   ;  \n   j   s   o   n   .
0000020   b       =       "   \   u   0   0   7   F   \   u   0   0   1
0000040   F   \   u   0   0   9   F   \   u   2   0   2   8   "   ;  \n
0000060
```

(`cat -A` on a longer run shows every line ending in `$` with no `^M`, no trailing
spaces.)

There are exactly five value *forms*:

| JSON type | Rendered as |
|---|---|
| number  | the raw input token, byte-for-byte (§1) |
| `true`  | `true` |
| `false` | `false` |
| `null`  | `null` |
| string  | double-quoted, gron-specific escaping (§3) |
| object  | `{}` — always, empty or not (§6) |
| array   | `[]` — always, empty or not (§6) |

---

## 1. Numbers — echoed **verbatim**, never reformatted

**Rule: the number value is copied byte-for-byte from the input token.** No
normalization of any kind: exponent letter case is preserved, `+` in the exponent
is preserved, trailing/leading zeros are preserved, `-0` stays `-0`, arbitrary
precision and arbitrary exponent magnitude are preserved, and no float64
conversion/rounding ever occurs.

```
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1e10,"d":1E10,"e":1e+10,"f":3.0e2,"g":-1,"h":-0,"i":1.0,"j":0.30000000000000004}' | /workspace/executable -
json = {};
json.a = 1;
json.b = 1.5;
json.c = 1e10;
json.d = 1E10;
json.e = 1e+10;
json.f = 3.0e2;
json.g = -1;
json.h = -0;
json.i = 1.0;
json.j = 0.30000000000000004;
exit=0
```

Note in particular: `1E10` → `1E10` (not `1e10`), `1e+10` → `1e+10` (the `+` is
kept), `3.0e2` → `3.0e2` (not `300`), `1.0` → `1.0` (not `1`), `-0` → `-0` (not
`0`), `0.30000000000000004` → unchanged (no shortest-round-trip reformatting).

Beyond int64 / float64 range — still verbatim, still exit 0, no overflow error:

```
$ echo '{"a":123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890,"b":1e400,"c":1e-400,"d":9223372036854775808,"e":-9223372036854775809,"f":1e1000000,"g":0e0,"h":-0.0,"i":0.0000}' | /workspace/executable -
json = {};
json.a = 123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890;
json.b = 1e400;
json.c = 1e-400;
json.d = 9223372036854775808;
json.e = -9223372036854775809;
json.f = 1e1000000;
json.g = 0e0;
json.h = -0.0;
json.i = 0.0000;
exit=0
```

`1e400` would be `+Inf` as a float64 and `1e-400` would be `0`; neither is
converted. Huge integers past 2^63 are not clamped or turned into floats.

Whitespace around a number is not part of the token:

```
$ printf '{"a":   1e10   }' > sp.json && /workspace/executable sp.json
json = {};
json.a = 1e10;
```

### 1.1 Randomized verbatim proof

3312 distinct valid JSON number tokens (cross product of integer parts up to
500 digits incl. `9`×500, `-`×`9`×500, `1`+`0`×400, `9223372036854775807/8`,
`18446744073709551616`; fraction parts up to 400 digits, `.1000000000000000055511151231257827`,
`.30000000000000004`; exponents `e0 E0 e+0 e-0 e10 E10 e+10 e-10 e308 e309 e400
e-400 e-324 e1000000 E-1000000 e+000000000010 e`+`9`×20, `e-`+`9`×20) were emitted
as one big array and run through `/workspace/executable --no-sort -`:

```
parsed 3312 of 3312
mismatches: 0
```

Conclusion: **zero** normalization. Reimplementation must retain the literal
source bytes of the number token (e.g. Go: `json.Decoder.UseNumber()` and print
the `json.Number` string).

### 1.2 Invalid number syntax → parser errors

All go to **stderr**, produce **empty stdout**, and exit **3**. Message is always
`failed to form statements: ` + the Go `encoding/json` syntax error, then `\n`.

| Input | stderr (byte-for-byte, minus trailing `\n`) |
|---|---|
| `{"a":01}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '1' after object key:value pair` |
| `{"a":00}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '0' after object key:value pair` |
| `{"a":-01}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '1' after object key:value pair` |
| `{"a":.5}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '.' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":5.}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '}' after decimal point in numeric literal` |
| `{"a":+1}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '+' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":1e}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '}' in exponent of numeric literal` |
| `{"a":0x10}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'x' after object key:value pair` |
| `{"a":Infinity}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'I' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":NaN}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'N' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":1.2.3}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character '.' after object key:value pair` |

Note the leading-zero cases: `01` is diagnosed as *"invalid character '1' after
object key:value pair"* (the `0` parses as a complete value, then `1` is
unexpected) — **not** as a "leading zero" error.

Command used for each row (example):

```
$ printf '{"a":01}' | /workspace/executable - ; echo "exit=$?"
failed to form statements: invalid character '1' after object key:value pair
exit=3
```

---

## 2. Booleans and `null`

Rendered as the bare lowercase literals `true`, `false`, `null`. No quotes.

```
$ printf '{"t":true,"f":false,"n":null,"arr":[true,false,null]}' | /workspace/executable -
json = {};
json.arr = [];
json.arr[0] = true;
json.arr[1] = false;
json.arr[2] = null;
json.f = false;
json.n = null;
json.t = true;
exit=0
```

Only the exact lowercase spellings are accepted by the parser (all → stderr,
empty stdout, exit 3):

| Input | stderr |
|---|---|
| `{"a":True}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'T' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":TRUE}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'T' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":Null}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'N' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":NULL}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'N' looking for beginning of value` |
| `{"a":nil}` | `failed to form statements: invalid character 'i' in literal null (expecting 'u')` |

---

## 3. Strings — exact escaping rules

Output is `"` + escaped body + `"`. The escaping is applied to the **decoded**
string (see §3.3: input is fully canonicalized), and is **not** Go
`encoding/json`'s default (it differs on `<`, `>`, `&`, U+007F and U+0080–U+009F).

### 3.1 The complete rule (exhaustively verified)

```
for each code point cp in the decoded string:
    0x08 -> \b
    0x09 -> \t
    0x0A -> \n
    0x0C -> \f
    0x0D -> \r
    0x22 -> \"          (")
    0x5C -> \\          (\)
    else if cp <= 0x1F                  -> \uXXXX
    else if 0x7F <= cp <= 0x9F          -> \uXXXX
    else if cp == 0x2028 or cp == 0x2029 -> \uXXXX
    else                                -> the code point's raw UTF-8 bytes
```

`\uXXXX` form: lowercase literal `u`, **always exactly 4 hex digits**, hex digits
**UPPERCASE** (`A`–`F`). No `\u{...}`, no surrogate pairs are ever emitted (see
§3.2 — nothing above U+2029 is ever escaped, so the 4-digit form always suffices).

### 3.2 Exhaustive Unicode sweep — the escape set is exactly 69 code points

Method: for each of the **1,112,064** Unicode scalar values (U+0000–U+10FFFF minus
the surrogate block D800–DFFF), emit a JSON array element containing that single
code point written as a `\uXXXX` escape (surrogate pair for astral planes), run
`/workspace/executable --no-sort -` in 0x8000-sized chunks, and compare the
returned value body against the code point's raw UTF-8 encoding.
Script: `/tmp/probe/work-01/sweep_all.py`.

```
$ python3 /tmp/probe/work-01/sweep_all.py
total code points tested: 1112064
number NOT passed through as raw UTF-8: 69
U+0000..U+0007  n=8  sample=b'\\u0000' .. b'\\u0007'
U+0008..U+000A  n=3  sample=b'\\b' .. b'\\n'
U+000B..U+000B  n=1  sample=b'\\u000B' .. b'\\u000B'
U+000C..U+000D  n=2  sample=b'\\f' .. b'\\r'
U+000E..U+001F  n=18  sample=b'\\u000E' .. b'\\u001F'
U+0022..U+0022  n=1  sample=b'\\"' .. b'\\"'
U+005C..U+005C  n=1  sample=b'\\\\' .. b'\\\\'
U+007F..U+009F  n=33  sample=b'\\u007F' .. b'\\u009F'
U+2028..U+2029  n=2  sample=b'\\u2028' .. b'\\u2029'
```

That is the **complete** list. Every other scalar value — including every one
requested in the task — is emitted as raw UTF-8 bytes:

| Code point | Output value body | Escaped? |
|---|---|---|
| U+0020 SPACE | `" "` | no |
| U+0027 `'` | `"'"` | **no** |
| U+002F `/` | `"/"` | **no** |
| U+003C `<` | `"<"` | **no** |
| U+003E `>` | `">"` | **no** |
| U+0026 `&` | `"&"` | **no** |
| U+007E `~` | `"~"` | no |
| U+007F DEL | `""` | **yes** |
| U+0080..U+009F (C1) | `""` … `""` | **yes** |
| U+00A0 NBSP | raw `c2 a0` | no |
| U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN | raw `c2 ad` | no |
| U+00FF | raw `c3 bf` | no |
| U+0100 | raw `c4 80` | no |
| U+2027 | raw `e2 80 a7` | no |
| U+2028 LINE SEP | `" "` | **yes** |
| U+2029 PARA SEP | `" "` | **yes** |
| U+202A LRE | raw `e2 80 aa` | no |
| U+FEFF BOM/ZWNBSP | raw `ef bb bf` | no |
| U+FFFD REPLACEMENT | raw `ef bf bd` | no |
| U+FFFF (noncharacter) | raw `ef bf bf` | no |
| U+10000 | raw `f0 90 80 80` | no |
| U+10FFFF | raw `f4 8f bf bf` | no |

Characterization of the escape predicate: it is exactly
`unicode.IsControl(r)` (Unicode category **Cc** = U+0000–U+001F ∪ U+007F–U+009F)
**plus** U+2028 and U+2029, **plus** the JSON-mandatory `"` and `\`, with the
seven short escapes taking priority. Note U+000B (VT) has **no** short escape and
comes out as ``, and `/` is **not** escaped. Category **Cf** (format:
U+00AD, U+200B, U+202A, U+FEFF, U+E0001…), **Co** (private use), **Cn**
(unassigned/noncharacters, e.g. U+FFFF) are all passed through raw.

Hex-digit case verified byte-level with `od -c` (see §0): `\ u 0 0 7 F`,
`\ u 0 0 1 F`, `\ u 0 0 9 F`, `\ u 2 0 2 8` — the `u` is lowercase, `F` uppercase.

for printable code points, which proves canonicalization. Direct demo:

```
$ printf '{"a":"A/<>&' é"}' | /workspace/executable -

json.a = "A/<>&' é";

(lowercase hex) → output `` (**uppercase** hex — case is normalized);
input `é` → output raw UTF-8 `c3 a9`. Also:

| Input string body | Output value body |
|---|---|
| `\/` | `"/"` |
| `\b\f\n\r\t\"\\/` | `"\b\f\n\r\t\"\\/"` (short escapes round-trip; `/` unescaped) |
| `😀` | `"😀"` (raw `f0 9f 98 80`) |
| `😀` | `"😀"` (input hex case irrelevant) |
| `  ` | `"  "` |

```

**Rule:** the input is UTF-8-decoded with Go's semantics; every byte that is not
part of a valid, shortest-form, in-range (≤ U+10FFFF, non-surrogate) UTF-8
sequence is replaced by **one U+FFFD per offending byte**. The resulting U+FFFD
is then emitted as raw bytes `ef bf bd` (it is not in the escape set). **No
error, no warning, exit 0.**

```

| Description | raw bytes in string | stdout value body |
|---|---|---|
| lone 0x80 | `80` | `"\xef\xbf\xbd"` (1× FFFD) |
| lone 0x81 | `81` | 1× FFFD |
| lone 0xBF | `bf` | 1× FFFD |
| 0xC3 with no continuation | `c3` | 1× FFFD |
| 0xC3 then `a` | `c3 61` | `"\xef\xbf\xbda"` (FFFD + `a`) |
| valid 2-byte (é) | `c3 a9` | `"\xc3\xa9"` (unchanged) |
| overlong NUL | `c0 80` | 2× FFFD |
| overlong 3-byte | `e0 80 80` | 3× FFFD |
| overlong `/` | `c0 af` | 2× FFFD |
| CESU surrogate U+D800 | `ed a0 80` | 3× FFFD |
| CESU surrogate U+DFFF | `ed bf bf` | 3× FFFD |
| 5-byte sequence | `f8 88 80 80 80` | 5× FFFD |

| truncated 4-byte | `f0 9f 98` | 3× FFFD |
